Pulmonary Disorders

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

COPD in the ED is two problems: chronic baseline limitation that may be underdiagnosed, and acute exacerbation where oxygen, bronchodilators, infection treatment, and ventilatory support must be titrated without worsening hypercapnia.

Board trap: Do not reflexively chase 100% oxygen saturation in COPD exacerbation; target oxygenation and reassess ventilation.

CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

COPD is a common preventable and treatable disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation. Tobacco smoke is the major risk factor, but occupational dust, chemical exposure, indoor biomass smoke, air pollution, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency also matter. Many patients are underdiagnosed because slow exertional decline is attributed to aging or deconditioning.

In the ED, suspected COPD is a clinical working diagnosis, but definitive COPD requires spirometry after the acute episode. Acute dyspnea still demands a differential diagnosis, not automatic labeling as COPD.

CHRONIC COMPENSATED OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Chronic airway inflammation narrows small airways, increases mucus, impairs clearance, and destroys alveolar-capillary support. Chronic bronchitis adds mucus and secretion burden; emphysema adds loss of elastic recoil, hyperinflation, V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular strain. Loss of expiratory flow reserve is why small physiologic insults can produce large ED presentations.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Baseline COPD symptoms include chronic progressive dyspnea, cough, and sputum production. Severe disease may show tachypnea, accessory muscle use, wheeze, prolonged expiration, coarse crackles, pursed-lip breathing, cyanosis, cachexia, tremor, confusion, or signs of cor pulmonale. Exam and ABG can be deceptively stable in compensated disease.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis is suspected from symptoms and exposure history and confirmed later with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC less than 0.7. Chest radiograph may show hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, increased AP diameter, and decreased vascular markings, but imaging does not replace spirometry. Radiography is most useful for complications or alternate diagnoses.

TREATMENT

Oxygen

Long-term oxygen improves mortality in chronic qualifying hypoxemia. Chronic outpatient oxygen thresholds differ from ED stabilization, but the principle is the same: correct tissue oxygenation while monitoring CO2 retention.

Pharmacotherapy

Maintenance therapy uses inhaled bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids for selected exacerbation-prone patients, and long-acting agents based on symptoms and exacerbation risk. Acute ED therapy uses short-acting agents first; chronic maintenance choices are revisited after stabilization.

Secretion Mobilization

Hydration, humidification, and mobilization can help secretion clearance. Routine antitussives and mucolytics have limited ED value and should not distract from treating airflow obstruction and infection triggers.

Smoking Cessation, Pulmonary Rehabilitation, and Vaccination

Smoking cessation is the only intervention that reduces both FEV1 decline and mortality. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and quality of life. Pneumococcal and influenza vaccination reduce infectious triggers.

ACUTE EXACERBATIONS OF CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE

Acute exacerbations worsen dyspnea, sputum volume, or sputum purulence beyond baseline. Infections are common, but pollutants, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, heart failure, ACS, arrhythmia, and medication changes are frequent alternatives or co-triggers.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Hypoxemia is the most immediately threatening feature. Increased work of breathing, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, altered mental status, and paradoxical breathing warn of fatigue. Pulsus paradoxus and a prolonged expiratory phase reflect severe obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation.

DIAGNOSIS

Evaluate oxygen saturation, ventilation, sputum changes, triggers, chest radiograph, ECG, and selected labs based on severity. ABG is important in severe exacerbation, suspected hypercapnia, NIV decisions, or intubation risk. Chest radiograph looks for pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema, malignancy, or alternative diagnosis. A normal or familiar COPD film does not rule out PE or ACS when the clinical story fits.

TREATMENT

Oxygen

Administer controlled oxygen, commonly targeting saturation 88% to 92% or PaO2 60 to 70 mm Hg. If high oxygen concentrations are required or mental status worsens, reassess CO2 and acid-base status. Oxygen treats hypoxemia, but ventilation treats hypercapnic respiratory failure.

B2-Adrenergic Agonists

Short-acting beta2-agonists are first-line for acute bronchospasm. Use MDI with spacer when the patient can cooperate; nebulized or continuous delivery helps severe airflow obstruction. Monitor tachycardia and arrhythmias, but avoid undertreating bronchospasm.

Anticholinergics

Ipratropium is best combined with SABA in exacerbations. Its benefit is modest but useful, and side effects are usually limited to dry mouth or unpleasant taste.

Corticosteroids

Systemic corticosteroids shorten recovery, improve lung function, and reduce treatment failure. Short courses, often 5 to 7 days, are usually sufficient; IV therapy is reserved for vomiting, shock, or impaired absorption.

Antibiotics

Antibiotics are indicated for moderate or severe illness when infection is likely, especially increased sputum purulence, increased sputum volume, or fever. Coverage commonly targets Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, with Pseudomonas coverage for selected high-risk patients.

Noninvasive and Invasive Mechanical Ventilation

NIV is first-line ventilatory support for COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis, hypercapnia, severe dyspnea, accessory muscle use, and persistent hypoxemia despite oxygen. Contraindications include arrest, inability to protect airway, severe instability, active vomiting, facial trauma, and poor cooperation. Early NIV prevents intubation when used in the right patient; delayed intubation harms the wrong patient.

Table 70-5

Indications for intubation with mechanical ventilation.

Intubate for NIV failure, respiratory or cardiac arrest, respiratory failure, decreased consciousness, aspiration, secretion failure, persistent hypoxemia, hypotension, or hemodynamic instability. Ventilator management prioritizes normoxia, long expiratory time, low respiratory rate, and tolerance of hypercapnia if pH is acceptable. Dynamic hyperinflation and intrinsic PEEP cause hypotension and difficulty triggering the ventilator.

Other Therapies

Routine magnesium, methylxanthines, and heliox are not recommended for standard COPD exacerbation. High-flow nasal cannula may help oxygenation in selected patients, but NIV remains the preferred support for hypercapnic respiratory failure when tolerated.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Disposition depends on severity, response to therapy, oxygen need, CO2/pH status, comorbidities, social support, and recurrence risk. Admit patients with marked symptom increase, failure of initial therapy, significant comorbidity, arrhythmia/heart failure, older age, frequent relapse, or inadequate home support. ICU admission is needed for severe dyspnea refractory to initial therapy, worsening mental status, worsening respiratory acidosis, NIV requirement, hemodynamic instability, or need for invasive ventilation.

Safe discharge requires improved symptoms, stable oxygenation near baseline, reliable inhaler technique, bronchodilator access, steroid/antibiotic plan when indicated, smoking cessation counseling, return precautions, and follow-up. Observation can be useful, but persistent hypoxemia, tachypnea, drowsiness, confusion, or worsening acidosis is not an observation-unit problem.
